lines.dialogue: An hour after first light at the Silent Pond. The lotus ring holds its flowers still, and the notice on the warehouse threshold carries a seal and no signature.
It says the pond is to be drained for sanitation. Everything in it must be read onto a district slate by the morning bell, and the clerk comes at noon.

On the diving stone the boy lays out his morning: a brass buckle, heavy, off a mill man's belt; one small left shoe; a button from a novice's shoulder; two coins kept apart, because the pond throws back whatever is round.
One word a day. Today's word is not yours to ask.
lines.stage_directions: Phra Kam sits at the muddy edge, the black notebook open on his knee.

lines.dialogue: If no one reads the pond's things into the record, the clerk writes 'uncatalogued sacred rubbish' on the slate, and the drainers do the rest.
Decide what the district is allowed to know, clerk. You have until the morning bell.
Palm up, arm straight, no bow. He handles brass the way his mother handles rice. That is how you know it mattered. The pond is not a bank. It keeps nothing and owes nothing.
lines.stage_directions: He watches the boy's hands, not the buckle.

lines.dialogue: The clerk's slate turns it into a bank whether it wills or not. On his page the buckle is brass, two ounces, one entry, and the district knows the stoker by weight.
The stoker was a man the grammar mill fired in the rains. The mill burned a week later, and his son threw the buckle in to feel lighter.
The boy closes his fist, opens it over Lek's palm: a rusted spoon, twin to the one Phra Kam eats with.
A thing given to the water is not given away, clerk. It comes back as rain, as rice, as a boy with a spoon. The district counts what it can see. The water counts the rest.
Then the slate is a prayer book and I am the monk ordered to read it. Tell me what to read, Phra Kam.

line.dialogue: The slate or the water, clerk. Read the pond into the officer's record and the pond becomes his account. Stand with the water and the district learns your name instead of its contents. My notebook has room for either word.

choices.description: I will take the clerk's slate at noon and write the inventory myself, every buckle and button, so the pond enters the record under my hand.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam write 'received' and close the book before I hand the slate back.
I see Phra Kam turn his bowl upside down on the stone, and he says the pond is closed to him too.

choices.description: I will stand with Phra Kam and tell the clerk the pond is temple ground, and its things are not district property to be counted.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam slide the notebook toward me, open to today's page: 'refused,' underlined once.
I see Phra Kam pick up his mat and move to the far edge, where the clerk can watch him not watching.

choices.description: I will ask the boy to give the slate to the pond before noon, and tell the clerk the pond took his list as it takes everything.

line.dialogue: I see the boy come up with the slate dripping, and Phra Kam almost smile before he writes 'received.'
I see the clerk fish the slate out himself, dripping and blank, and Phra Kam write nothing at all.

lines.dialogue: Midday at the ash alcove. The Chant Ledger nailed to the wall has never held one name, and the canal grate runs under the shelf.
'Light, a child. Heavy, a woodcutter. Warm, yesterday's.' She lifts each jar an inch and sets it back. 'My hands know the shelf. The district wants the shelf to know it back.'
The order came with the drainage notice. At dusk the canal takes every jar with no name in the ledger.
Forty years I have kept what the fire left, and tonight the district counts it as silt.
I do not chant for the nameless. No name, no merit. Ask the keeper how long I have held that line.
The only thing necessary to save the warm jar is a name in that ledger and one chant at dark. That is all the law asks.
The new jar has no label. It is still warm at the rim.
I write my names in lemon juice and lamp smoke. They show when the jar sweats. The ledger wants ink, and ink is heavier than my names.
A boatman brought it before dawn and did not wait for a receipt. The canal will take it back the same way, unwitnessed.
If no one claims them, I claim them. Is that sin or service?
A name is the only coin the dead can spend, keeper. Do not mint them fakes.
Then true coin or none. Keeper, is there a name in this alcove that is yours to give?

line.dialogue: The canal bell rings at dusk, young clerk. Write a borrowed name in the ledger and the jar stays on my shelf. Pour your own water for it and the ledger stays blank and the canal decides. Or find me a truer door. My arms cannot stop the canal.

choices.description: I will not write a false name. I will carry merit-water from the blessing ghat and pour it for the nameless jar myself, and let the canal decide what the ledger cannot hold.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam take one grain of rice from his bowl and set it on the jar's lid before the water falls.
I see Phra Kam hold his bowl shut while the water falls, and the jar lid stays dry as dust.

choices.description: I will take a name from the canal register, a real name, a real dead man with no jar of his own, and write it in the Chant Ledger so the warm jar can stay.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam read the borrowed name twice and write 'received' before the ink dries.
I see Phra Kam close the ledger with his palm and shake his head at the shelf.

choices.description: I will ask the keeper to claim the jar as her own kin before the officer. A claimed jar is paperwork enough, and her name on it is true.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam bow to the keeper, once, from the waist, and write 'received' in letters readable from the door.
I see the keeper's hand shake on the claim, and Phra Kam turn away before the ink sets.

lines.dialogue: Evening at the Donation Mirror. The tax clerk from the rice ledger unbars the weighing hut and sets his scales on the floating tray.
Three bowls sit under the tray: gold, bone, teeth. The gold goes to the temple, the bone to the families, the teeth back to the water. That is the whole of my accounts.
The widow is on the third step with a golden lotus. Her husband died in prison. She will not give it to the glass. She wants the water under the mirror.
The temple pays me by the grain. What my scale cannot hold will be estimated, and estimation rounds to the temple.
I keep my back to the glass. It knows my face and would charge me for the showing.
The clerk wants one answer by the second bell: the weight of everything the mirror took this month.
The rich drop gold and see saints. The poor drop rice and see ghosts. I polish the glass so both can weep in it.
Rice by the dry measure, clerk. Offerings by the same scale. The law does not weigh tears.
He expects us to believe a golden lotus weighs like rice because one scale says so.
In Bangkok I passed every Pali exam and failed the test of silence. I spoke against a man who bought a hall of merit to wash his son's murder debt. My superiors silenced me, and I walked north.
Then your silence is not peace, Phra Kam. It is the one debt you still refuse to pay.
The mirror does not forgive, clerk. It refuses to remember the price. Men call that mercy, and weep.

line.dialogue: The second bell is close, young clerk. Speak your learned words and quote the temple law, and the weighing stops for tonight, and the widow waits dry. Carry her water first and my scale finishes its number while you pour. Or show me a third door. My scales only know what they know.

choices.description: I will leave the argument and carry the evening water to the widow myself, and let the scale finish its number while the pouring still matters.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam dip his spoon in the widow's cup before he eats, and write 'received.'
I see Phra Kam eat before the widow's cup is filled, and the page stays blank.

choices.description: I will make the clerk weigh by the temple's own rule: rice by the dry measure, offerings by no measure, and read the rule aloud until the whole landing hears it.

line.dialogue: I see the clerk's scale hand stop in the air, and Phra Kam write 'received' before the rule is half-read.
I see the clerk finish the number anyway and write it larger, and Phra Kam close the book.

choices.description: I will ask the tender for the mirror's drawer key, and take the lotus and this month's rice out of the scales' reach entirely.

line.dialogue: I see the tender turn the key, and Phra Kam set his palm flat on the drawer once, like a seal.
I see the tender refuse the key with a shake of his head, and the drawer stay shut on nothing.

lines.dialogue: Night on the School Veranda. The bowls are in a row, and the tax clerk waits at the rail with three folded papers.
The pond, the shelf, the glass. One witness-signature on all three by the morning bell. Sign, and the district forgets your name. Refuse, and it learns yours.
The warm jar rides on my hip. Whatever name it carries, it rides inside tonight.
The lotus rides in my sleeve until the temple forgets to ask for it.
The pond boy is on the steps. He sets two rusted spoons on the rail, side by side, and sits on his heels.
Three papers, one jar, one lotus, two spoons. The district counts things, clerk. It has never once counted what they meant.
The officer does not judge ponds or jars, young clerk. He judges whether the veranda stands with the district or against it.
You have the words to fight one paper, clerk, and the manners to sign all three. My notebook says words cost more than you think.
Then let the officer judge the veranda by the word it sends back.
Every sink is a receipt, clerk. The water wrote my two words before I was born. I copy them out fair, that is all.
One pen, three papers, the morning bell. Whatever we feed the district, we feed it tonight.
The boat takes the papers at the bell. After that, the district writes the veranda itself.

line.dialogue: Last choice, clerk, and it is yours. Fight the papers with your words and spend the officer's face. Sign them, and keep his face, and lose the fight you love. Or send my word down the river in place of your name, and let the district make of it what it will.

choices.description: I will sign all three papers and return the clerk's pen with both hands, and keep the officer's face for the veranda.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam write 'received' in the margin of my signature and tap the page twice with his pencil.
I see Phra Kam close the notebook on my signature like a lid on something cooling.

choices.description: I will refuse the signature and give the reasons one by one: the pond is temple ground, the jars are temple dead, the mirror is temple glass.

line.dialogue: I see Phra Kam listen to the last reason and write 'refused' under the clerk's third question.
I see the clerk gather his papers before my reasons are spent, and Phra Kam's page stay blank.

choices.description: I will ask Phra Kam to write his word on all three papers, and let the officer carry a monk's receipt or refusal in place of my name.

line.dialogue: I see the clerk carry the three papers away like relics, and Phra Kam eat from his rusted spoon for the first time since morning.
I see the clerk shake his head at the monk's word and write 'uncooperative' small in the corner, and the spoons stay on the rail.
